case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a failure to disclose information required under Item 303 of SEC Regulation S-K can independently support a private securities fraud action under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5, even in the absence of an otherwise misleading statement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; Rule 10b-5 promulgated thereunder; Item 303 of SEC Regulation S-K (Management's Discussion and Analysis - MD&A disclosure requirements); Sections 11 and 12(a)(2) of the Securities Act of 1933
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Macquarie Infrastructure Corp. and supporting amici (including SIFMA, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, Washington Legal Foundation, Atlantic Legal Foundation, and Society for Corporate Governance) argue that the Second Circuit erred by holding that a mere failure to comply with Item 303 disclosure requirements can sustain a private securities fraud claim under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 without an otherwise misleading affirmative statement. Petitioners contend that pure omissions — standing alone — cannot constitute actionable fraud under Rule 10b-5 absent a duty to disclose arising from a specific misleading statement or half-truth, and that the Second Circuit's ruling creates an impermissible circuit split with the Third, Ninth, and Eleventh Circuits. They further argue that allowing Item 303 omissions to independently ground securities fraud liability would dramatically expand private litigation exposure for public companies, chill legitimate business disclosures, and effectively transform a regulatory disclosure obligation into a private right of action beyond what Congress intended.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Moab Partners, L.P. argues that the Second Circuit correctly held that Item 303 of Regulation S-K creates an affirmative duty to disclose known trends and uncertainties in MD&A filings, and that a violation of this duty — when combined with adequate and independent pleading of all other required Rule 10b-5 elements (including scienter, materiality, reliance, and loss causation) — can support a private securities fraud claim. Respondent Moab Partners contends that the omission of material information required by Item 303 renders public filings misleading by omission, satisfying the misrepresentation or omission element of Rule 10b-5. Respondent Barclays Capital Inc. supports vacatur but notes that the Court's ruling will also affect the viability of claims against it under Sections 11 and 12(a)(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, which are premised on the same alleged Item 303 disclosure failures, suggesting the Court should carefully consider the broader implications of its holding across multiple securities law provisions.
